books.title: Exploring Society: India and Beyond (Social Science Textbook for Grade 6)
books.edition: First Edition June 2024; reprinted February 2025 and February 2026 (the PDF carries no 'Reprint 2026-27' text)

source.method: chapter titles from the book's Contents page; topics from each chapter PDF's section headings

topics.title: A Map and Its Components
objectives: Student can explain what a map is and how it is used to find places
Student can name the three main components of a map: distance (scale), direction and symbols
Student can use the cardinal and intermediate directions and conventional symbols to read a map
visualIdeas: a compass rose with the eight directions
a small map with a scale bar and a legend of conventional symbols

topics.title: Understanding Coordinates
objectives: Student can explain that a globe is a model of the Earth and that a grid of coordinates fixes any location
Student can locate a square on a grid, such as a chessboard, using a pair of coordinates
visualIdeas: a chessboard with rows and columns labelled and a piece located by its coordinates

topics.title: Latitudes
objectives: Student can describe latitudes as imaginary lines running east to west, parallel to the Equator, measured in degrees north or south
Student can relate latitude to climate and name the Northern and Southern Hemispheres
visualIdeas: a globe with the Equator and parallels of latitude marked

topics.title: Longitudes
objectives: Student can describe longitudes as imaginary lines from pole to pole measured in degrees east or west of the Prime Meridian at Greenwich
Student can use latitude and longitude together to give the location of a place
Student can explain that ancient Indian astronomers used a prime meridian of their own, the madhya rekha through Ujjayini
visualIdeas: a globe with meridians and the Greenwich Prime Meridian highlighted
a map of the Ujjayini meridian with ancient cities on it

topics.title: Understanding Time Zones
objectives: Student can explain that local time changes by one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude
Student can explain standard time and why Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time
Student can explain what happens to the date when crossing the International Date Line at about 180 degrees longitude
visualIdeas: a world strip of time zones with clocks at 15-degree intervals
a globe centred on India showing standard times of a few countries

topics.title: The Distribution of Water and Land on the Earth
objectives: Student can explain that most of the Earth's surface is covered by water
Student can compare the share of land in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres
visualIdeas: the Earth seen from space centred on the Indian Ocean

topics.title: Oceans
objectives: Student can name and locate the major oceans on a world map
Student can explain that the oceans are interconnected
visualIdeas: a world map with the oceans labelled and their connections shown

topics.title: Oceans and Disasters
objectives: Student can explain that the monsoon rains India depends on originate over the ocean
Student can describe disasters that oceans can give rise to, such as storms and tsunamis
visualIdeas: clouds rising from the ocean and moving over land as monsoon rain
a tsunami wave approaching a coast

topics.title: Continents
objectives: Student can name and locate the seven continents in the most common count
Student can explain that continents may be counted in different ways
Student can define an island and give examples
visualIdeas: a world map with the seven continents coloured
an island surrounded by ocean

topics.title: Oceans and Life
objectives: Student can explain the role of oceans in the water cycle, in producing oxygen and in the world's climate
Student can describe the marine life oceans support and how human activity threatens it
Student can suggest why oceans need our collective protection
visualIdeas: an ocean food web from tiny organisms to whales
plastic waste floating in the sea

topics.title: Introduction to Landforms
objectives: Student can name the three main types of landforms: mountains, plateaus and plains
Student can explain terms such as altitude used to describe landforms
visualIdeas: a cross section showing a mountain, a plateau and a plain side by side

topics.title: Mountains
objectives: Student can describe the physical features of mountains and the mountain environment
Student can describe life in the mountains, including terrace farming, herding and tourism
Student can explain the challenges and opportunities of living in the mountains
visualIdeas: terrace farming cut into a mountain slope
a mountain village with herders and tourists

topics.title: Plateaus
objectives: Student can define a plateau as a raised landform with a more or less flat top and steep sides
Student can give examples such as the Tibetan Plateau and the Deccan Plateau and describe how people use plateaus
visualIdeas: a plateau with a flat top and steep sides
India map marking the Deccan Plateau

topics.title: Plains
objectives: Student can describe plains as flat, low-lying lands often formed by rivers
Student can explain why the first civilisations and large populations grew in fertile river plains such as the Ganga plain
Student can describe occupations of people in the plains
visualIdeas: the Ganga plain with rivers, fields and towns

topics.title: How Do We Learn About the Past?
objectives: Student can explain what history is and why we study the human past
Student can describe how palaeontologists, anthropologists and archaeologists study the past
visualIdeas: a museum hall with statues, coins and ornaments
an archaeologist digging up pots, beads and tools

topics.title: How Is Time Measured in History?
objectives: Student can place dates in BCE and CE on a timeline
Student can use units of historical time such as years, decades, centuries and millenniums
Student can explain that the Gregorian calendar is now used the world over
visualIdeas: a timeline with BCE on the left, CE on the right and year 1 in the middle

topics.title: What Are the Sources of History?
objectives: Student can name different sources of history: archaeological sources, inscriptions, manuscripts and other texts, and oral sources
Student can explain how sources help us reconstruct and interpret past events
Student can build a family tree from available sources
visualIdeas: a family tree with three generations and the source of each fact

topics.title: The Beginnings of Human History
objectives: Student can state that modern humans have lived on Earth for about 300,000 years
Student can describe how early humans lived, including their life in rock shelters
visualIdeas: rock-shelter paintings showing activities of early humans

topics.title: The First Crops
objectives: Student can explain how the end of the last Ice Age, about 12,000 years ago, improved living conditions for humans
Student can explain how humans began to settle down and cultivate crops
visualIdeas: a timeline from the last Ice Age to early farming settlements

topics.title: How Indians Named India
objectives: Student can explain names given to India or its regions by its ancient inhabitants, such as Sapta Sindhava, Jambudvipa and Bharata
Student can explain how Bharata became the name of India in most Indian languages
visualIdeas: a map of the northwest region labelled Sapta Sindhava
a list of names of India in different Indian languages

topics.title: How Foreigners Named India
objectives: Student can explain how the Persians' name Hindu came from the Sindhu river and was a geographical term
Student can trace how foreign names like Indoi and India were derived from Sindhu
visualIdeas: a word chain from Sindhu to Hindu to Indoi to India

topics.title: What Is a Civilisation?
objectives: Student can explain what makes a society a civilisation
Student can name the Indus, Harappan or Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation as one of the oldest in the world
visualIdeas: a checklist of the features of a civilisation

topics.title: From Village to City
objectives: Student can describe how villages grew into cities in the Harappan civilisation
Student can locate major Harappan sites and the Sarasvati river on a map
visualIdeas: a map of Harappan sites along the Indus and Sarasvati rivers

topics.title: Town-Planning
objectives: Student can describe the features of planned Harappan cities
Student can explain what town-planning tells us about the Harappans
visualIdeas: a plan of a Harappan city with streets laid out in a grid

topics.title: Water Management
objectives: Student can describe Harappan water management: bathing areas, covered drains, wells and reservoirs
Student can explain what reservoirs such as those at Dholavira reflect about the Harappans
visualIdeas: the drainage system at Lothal
a reservoir at Dholavira

topics.title: What Did the Harappans Eat?
objectives: Student can name the crops the Harappans grew: barley, wheat, some millets, sometimes rice, pulses and vegetables
Student can explain why settlements along rivers suited agriculture and that the Harappans were the first in Eurasia to grow cotton
Student can describe Harappan farming tools such as the plough
visualIdeas: a clay model of a Harappan plough
fields of barley, wheat and cotton beside a river settlement

topics.title: A Brisk Trade
objectives: Student can describe what the Harappans traded, such as carnelian beads and ornaments
Student can explain that the Harappans traded within their civilisation and with distant cultures
visualIdeas: trade routes from Harappan cities to distant regions with goods carried

topics.title: The Lives of the Ancients
objectives: Student can describe objects of daily use found at Harappan sites
Student can describe cultural and symbolic objects of the Harappans and compare them with things still used today
visualIdeas: Harappan pottery, ornaments, toys and seals displayed together

topics.title: The End or a New Beginning?
objectives: Student can explain the likely reasons for the decline of the Harappan cities, such as climatic and environmental changes
Student can describe how people moved to small rural settlements after the cities were abandoned
visualIdeas: an abandoned Harappan city beside small new villages

topics.title: The Vedas and Vedic Culture
objectives: Student can explain what the Vedas are and that they are India's earliest texts
Student can describe features of Vedic society, including the professions mentioned in Vedic texts
visualIdeas: a gurukula scene with students learning Vedic hymns orally

topics.title: Vedic Schools of Thought
objectives: Student can explain the Upanishadic ideas of brahman, atman, rebirth and karma
Student can name Vedanta and Yoga as schools of thought that grew out of the Vedas
Student can retell an Upanishadic story such as Nachiketa's quest and explain its message about asking questions
visualIdeas: a story panel of Nachiketa questioning Yama
a concept map linking the Vedas to Vedanta and Yoga

topics.title: Buddhism
objectives: Student can explain that Buddhism did not accept the authority of the Vedas and was founded by Siddhartha Gautama
Student can explain a few central ideas of Buddhism
visualIdeas: a map of places linked to the Buddha's life starting at Lumbini

topics.title: Jainism
objectives: Student can explain a few central ideas of Jainism
Student can explain the message of a Jain story from the chapter
visualIdeas: a chart of central Jain values with simple illustrations

topics.title: Folk and Tribal Roots
objectives: Student can explain what a tribe is
Student can describe how tribal belief systems regard the land as sacred and how they have interacted with Hinduism
visualIdeas: tribal art beside a hill and a river that a tribal community regards as sacred

chapters.title: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'

topics.title: A Rich Diversity
objectives: Student can describe India's diversity in landscapes, people, languages, dresses, foods, festivals and customs
Student can explain the idea of unity in diversity
visualIdeas: a train journey across India with changing landscapes, dress and languages

topics.title: Food for All
objectives: Student can describe the diversity of Indian food across regions
Student can name staple grains common to almost every part of India: cereals such as rice and wheat, millets such as bajra, jowar and ragi, and pulses
visualIdeas: an India map of cereals and pulses from different regions

topics.title: Textiles and Clothing
objectives: Student can describe the variety of textiles and clothing across India
Student can explain how the sari, an unstitched length of cloth in hundreds of varieties, is a commonality across most of India
visualIdeas: famous saris such as Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Paithani placed on an India map

topics.title: Festivals Galore
objectives: Student can describe festivals celebrated in different parts of India
Student can explain, using Makara Sankranti, how similar festivals are celebrated across India at about the same time under different names such as Pongal, Lohri, Magh Bihu and Uttarayan
visualIdeas: an India map of the regional names of the mid-January harvest festival

topics.title: An Epic Spread
objectives: Student can explain how stories such as the Panchatantra have been adapted in almost every Indian language and travelled beyond India
Student can explain how the epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, spread across India in many versions and show unity in diversity
visualIdeas: a map of Panchatantra adaptations travelling from India to Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe

topics.title: Family
objectives: Student can explain why the family is the fundamental unit of society
Student can distinguish joint families from nuclear families
visualIdeas: a family tree of a joint family beside a nuclear family

topics.title: Roles and Responsibilities
objectives: Student can describe the roles and responsibilities of family members and how they support each other
Student can discuss rules followed in their family and why they matter
visualIdeas: a chart of family members and the tasks each takes on

topics.title: Community
objectives: Student can define a community and give examples of different kinds of community
Student can describe situations where community support makes a difference
Student can explain that communities are interdependent
visualIdeas: a neighbourhood map showing people helping one another

topics.title: Introduction: Why We Need Governance
objectives: Student can explain the meaning of governance and why rules are needed when many people live together
Student can explain why we need a government
visualIdeas: a crowded community with and without agreed rules

topics.title: Three Organs of Government
objectives: Student can name the three organs of government: legislative, executive and judiciary
Student can describe the role of each organ and why they need to work together
visualIdeas: a three-pillar diagram of legislature, executive and judiciary with their roles

topics.title: Three Levels of Government
objectives: Student can explain that the Indian government functions at three levels: national (Central), State and local
Student can match matters such as defence, police or local services to the right level of government
Student can explain that the President of India and a State's Governor are nominal heads, as illustrated by Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's presidency
visualIdeas: a three-tier chart of Central, State and local government with example functions

topics.title: Democracy
objectives: Student can explain the meaning of democracy and why it is important
Student can distinguish direct democracy from representative democracy
visualIdeas: citizens voting for representatives who then sit in an assembly

chapters.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 2: Local Government in Rural Areas

topics.title: Panchayati Raj System
objectives: Student can describe the Panchayati Raj system as a three-tier system of local government in rural areas
Student can explain why local self-government matters in a country with about 600,000 villages
visualIdeas: a three-tier diagram of Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad

topics.title: Gram Panchayat
objectives: Student can describe how the Gram Panchayat works, including the role of the Sarpanch and the Gram Sabha
Student can list functions of the Gram Panchayat
visualIdeas: a Gram Sabha meeting with villagers and the Sarpanch

topics.title: Exemplary Sarpanchs
objectives: Student can describe what exemplary Sarpanchs have done for their villages
Student can discuss what qualities make a good Gram Panchayat member
visualIdeas: before-and-after pictures of a village improved by its Panchayat

topics.title: Child-Friendly Panchayat Initiative
objectives: Student can explain the aim of the Child-Friendly Panchayat initiative
Student can suggest how children can take part in village governance
visualIdeas: children presenting suggestions at a Panchayat meeting

topics.title: Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad
objectives: Student can describe the Panchayat Samiti at the block level and the Zila Parishad at the district level
Student can explain the key functions of each tier of the Panchayati Raj system
visualIdeas: a district map divided into blocks and villages with the three tiers

chapters.title: Grassroots Democracy — Part 3: Local Government in Urban Areas

topics.title: Introduction: Governing Towns and Cities
objectives: Student can explain why towns and cities need their own local government
Student can give examples of civic problems handled at the local level in urban areas
visualIdeas: a city street with a leaking pipe, a blocked drain and a damaged road

topics.title: Urban Local Bodies: Types and Ward Committees
objectives: Student can distinguish a Municipal Corporation, a Municipal Council and a Nagar Panchayat by the population of the city or town they serve
Student can explain that cities are divided into wards and describe what ward committees do
visualIdeas: a chart of urban local bodies by city population
a city divided into wards with a ward committee

topics.title: Urban Local Bodies: Functions and Citizens' Duties
objectives: Student can list services provided by urban local bodies, such as those of the Indore Municipal Corporation, and how they are funded
Student can explain that urban local bodies have elected members who represent local citizens
Student can describe citizens' duties, such as segregating waste and reporting water leaks, that help urban local bodies work efficiently
visualIdeas: a services wheel of a Municipal Corporation
a citizen reporting a water leak

topics.title: Economic and Non-Economic Activities
objectives: Student can list the different activities people around them engage in
Student can distinguish economic activities, performed for money or money's worth, from non-economic activities
visualIdeas: a table of characters from a neighbourhood story and their activities, sorted into two groups

topics.title: Types of Economic Activities
objectives: Student can describe the ways people are paid for economic activities: salary, wage, fee and payment in kind
Student can explain value addition at each stage of turning something into another form
visualIdeas: a chain from raw material to finished product with value added at each step

topics.title: The Importance of Non-Economic Activities
objectives: Student can explain how non-economic activities contribute to social welfare and personal wellbeing
Student can explain seva, selfless service, and the strength of community participation
visualIdeas: volunteers at a community kitchen or cleanliness drive

topics.title: Primary Activities
objectives: Student can define primary activities as those that use natural resources directly
Student can give examples of primary activities such as farming, fishing and mining
visualIdeas: farming, fishing and mining scenes grouped as the primary sector

topics.title: Secondary Activities
objectives: Student can define secondary activities as those that turn raw materials into products
Student can explain how the secondary sector depends on the primary sector
visualIdeas: raw cotton turning into cloth in a mill

topics.title: Tertiary Activities
objectives: Student can define tertiary activities as services that support the other sectors
Student can give examples such as transport, banking and trade
visualIdeas: a truck, a bank and a shop grouped as the tertiary sector

topics.title: Interdependence Among Sectors
objectives: Student can explain how the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors depend on each other
Student can trace a product through all three sectors using the example of a dairy cooperative from farm to plate
visualIdeas: a flow diagram of milk from farm to processing plant to shop to home
